title: Distributed systems: guarantees under partial failure
description: Reason about replicated state, clocks, consistency, consensus, retries, and ownership using explicit failure models and event histories.

lessons.title: Safety, liveness, and partial failure
lessons.summary: State what must never happen and what must eventually happen
objectives: State what must never happen and what must eventually happen.
Explain why a timeout is not proof of a crash.
lessons.body:
## Core idea

Safety rules out bad outcomes such as two committed owners for one resource under the protocol contract. Liveness describes progress under stated conditions. Networks can delay, duplicate, reorder, or drop messages, and processes can pause or crash. A timeout cannot distinguish all of these cases. State whether faults are crash-only or include malicious behavior, and which timing assumptions are needed for progress.

## Worked example

A worker missing a heartbeat may be dead, partitioned, or paused. Starting a replacement can restore progress but creates overlapping ownership unless the resource enforces a current-owner protocol.

## Try it

Define safety and liveness for a replicated register. List behavior during a partition, a crash, and an indefinitely delayed message. State which failures your model excludes.

## Check your work

Each guarantee has assumptions. The design does not quietly promise bounded progress in a fully asynchronous model with arbitrary message delay.

## Primary reading

- [Raft extended paper](https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf)

lessons.title: Consistency guarantees are constraints on histories
lessons.summary: Use operation intervals to reason about linearizability
objectives: Use operation intervals to reason about linearizability.
Distinguish freshness from eventual convergence.
lessons.body:
## Core idea

A history records invocations and responses. Linearizability requires an order consistent with each operation’s semantics and real-time precedence between non-overlapping operations. Other guarantees can permit observations that linearizability excludes. Eventual convergence describes behavior after updates and communication settle under suitable assumptions; it does not by itself bound staleness or provide read-your-writes.

## Worked example

If write(7) returns before a later read begins, a linearizable single register without intervening writes cannot return its old value. If operations overlap, either order may be possible if it fits the complete history.

## Try it

Draw three read/write histories with overlapping operations. Decide whether each admits a legal linearization and mark the constraints imposed by completed writes.

## Check your work

A valid answer constructs a full legal order or identifies a contradiction. It does not declare every stale-looking concurrent read invalid without checking operation overlap.

## Primary reading

- [Raft extended paper](https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf)

lessons.title: Physical clocks and logical causality
lessons.summary: Distinguish wall-clock order from causal order
objectives: Distinguish wall-clock order from causal order.
Use logical clocks with explicit comparison limits.
lessons.body:
## Core idea

Physical clocks have offset and drift. They help with timestamps and time-based policies but do not automatically establish causal order. Lamport clocks respect happens-before in one direction; a larger Lamport value does not prove causation. Vector clocks can represent more causal information at greater metadata cost. A timestamp-based conflict policy must explain tie breaking and clock assumptions.

## Worked example

Two isolated writers can produce timestamps that disagree with real-time order if their clocks differ. Choosing the numerically later timestamp can discard an update without representing the user’s intended sequence.

### Follow the steps

Start each process at clock 0. A sends to B at time 1, then makes a local edit at time 2. B makes its own edit at time 1 before receiving A's message. On receive, B uses max(1, 1) + 1 = 2. B then sends to C at time 3. C has clock 0, so its receive is time 4.

A's send happened before C's receive through the message chain. A's local edit and B's local edit have no message path between them. Their timestamps differ, but the trace gives no causal ordering between those edits. Extend the trace by sending a reply from C to A and calculate A's receive timestamp.

## Try it

Assign Lamport timestamps to a three-process message trace. Identify causally ordered events and concurrent events, then explain what information the scalar clocks cannot recover.

## Check your work

Every send/receive edge advances time correctly. The explanation avoids reversing the implication from happens-before to scalar-clock order.

## Primary reading

Optional reading after the example and exercise.

- [Lamport, Time, Clocks, and the Ordering of Events](https://lamport.azurewebsites.net/pubs/time-clocks.pdf) · Read “The Partial Ordering” and “Logical Clocks” for the event relation and clock rules used above.

lessons.title: The partition forces a choice
lessons.body:
## The problem to understand

A replicated register is split into two network partitions. Clients can reach both sides. You require linearizable reads/writes and every request to a non-failed node to complete successfully without waiting for the partition to heal. Which statement is correct under an asynchronous partition model?

## The mental model

Those requirements cannot both be guaranteed during the partition. If both sides independently acknowledge conflicting writes and serve fresh linearizable reads, they cannot maintain one real-time-consistent register history without communication. Preserving linearizability requires some operations to wait or fail on a side that cannot safely coordinate.

This is a statement about behavior under partitions, not a rule that every system permanently chooses only two useful properties. Practical systems define consistency and availability contracts per operation and failure mode. Returning an error is operationally useful but does not satisfy the successful-response availability requirement stated here.

## Check your understanding

- Identify the incompatible requirements during a partition.
- Relate linearizability to one real-time-consistent history.
- Distinguish practical error handling from the stated availability definition.

## Think one step further

Which operations could remain available if the application only requires commutative increments?

## Primary reading

- [Raft · extended paper](https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf)
objectives: Identify the incompatible requirements during a partition.
Relate linearizability to one real-time-consistent history.

lessons.title: Leader replication, logs, and applied state
lessons.summary: Separate appended, committed, and applied entries
objectives: Separate appended, committed, and applied entries.
Explain why replication alone is not a consensus protocol.
lessons.body:
## Core idea

A leader can assign an order to log entries and replicate them, but safe leadership changes require rules about elections, prior entries, and commitment. Appending an entry on one server is different from committing it under the protocol, and applying it to a state machine is another step. Acknowledgement semantics should name which boundary has been reached.

## Worked example

A leader crashes after appending an entry locally but before obtaining the required replication. A replacement must not invent a guarantee that the uncommitted entry survived. Conversely, acknowledged committed state must remain represented under the protocol assumptions.

## Try it

Trace a three-node log through append, replication, commitment, application, and leader crash. Label when a client success response is allowed in your stated protocol.

## Check your work

The trace uses one coherent consensus rule set rather than majority counting alone. It distinguishes persisted log state from in-memory application state and addresses recovery.

## Primary reading

- [Raft extended paper](https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf)

lessons.title: Consensus needs election and commitment rules together
lessons.summary: Explain the role of terms and election restrictions
objectives: Explain the role of terms and election restrictions.
Trace a leader change without losing committed history.
lessons.body:
## Core idea

Raft separates leader election, log replication, and safety. Terms identify election epochs; votes and log freshness rules limit who can lead. A majority is essential but not sufficient as a standalone description of every commitment case. Membership changes and durable metadata also matter. Study the complete protocol before adapting one attractive rule in isolation.

## Worked example

A candidate with a shorter, older log cannot simply win by being the first reachable server. Voters compare log freshness under Raft’s rules, preserving the possibility that a new leader contains committed history.

### Follow the steps

A leads term 1. Entry 1 (set x=5) is on A and B and has committed. A appends entry 2 (set x=7) only to its own log and crashes before acknowledging that write. B starts an election in term 2 and votes for itself. C sees the new term and can vote for B because B's log is at least as up to date. B plus C is a majority.

B appends a term-2 entry at index 2, sends entries 1 and 2 to C as needed, and can commit index 2 once C acknowledges it. The abandoned write on A never became committed. When A rejoins, a matching prefix followed by a conflict at index 2 lets B repair A's log. Repeat the trace with C campaigning first.

## Try it

Work through a paper trace with three servers, one leader crash, and one follower behind. Identify votes, terms, log matching, and the point each entry can be committed.

## Check your work

Explain each decision with the specific rule. Include the current-term commitment restriction and persisted vote/term information rather than assuming any replicated entry is immediately safe.

## Primary reading

Optional reading after the example and exercise.

- [Raft paper, §5.2–5.4](https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf#page=5) · Focus on elections, log matching, and the election restriction.

lessons.title: Where must two quorums meet?
lessons.body:
## The problem to understand

A fixed group has N=7 replicas. A write is acknowledged by W=4 distinct replicas. What is the smallest read quorum R that is guaranteed to intersect every such write quorum? Count only set intersection; do not assume that intersection alone proves linearizability.

## The mental model

Read and write sets must satisfy `R + W > N`. With W=4 and N=7, the smallest R is 4. A read set of size 3 can be disjoint from a particular write set of size 4; a set of size 4 cannot.

Intersection is a combinatorial requirement, not a complete protocol. Correctness also depends on version selection, concurrent writes, partial writes, failure handling, membership changes, and repair. A system with sloppy quorums or dynamic replacement replicas may not preserve the assumed fixed-set intersection.

## Check your understanding

- Use the strict inequality R+W>N.
- Find the smallest integer satisfying it.
- Avoid claiming intersection alone proves linearizability.

## Think one step further

Why does a read that contacts four replicas but returns the first response not implement a four-replica read quorum?

## Primary reading

- [Raft · extended paper](https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf)
objectives: Use the strict inequality R+W>N.
Find the smallest integer satisfying it.

lessons.title: Both writes succeeded. One update vanished.
lessons.body:
## The problem to understand

Two clients read the same object `{version: 7, count: 10}` from a linearizable key-value store. Each computes count+1 and writes `{count: 11}`. Both writes succeed. Explain why linearizable individual operations do not make the read-modify-write sequence atomic. Provide two valid API-level repairs and describe the retry rule for one of them.

## The mental model

Each read and write can be individually linearizable while the multi-operation sequence interleaves. Both clients read 10 before either write, and the second write overwrites 11 with 11. The result reflects only one logical increment even though both write calls succeeded.

Use an atomic increment operation, or a conditional write comparing the previously read version. With compare-and-swap, exactly one update based on version 7 succeeds; the other must reread the current version and recompute before retrying. Merely resending the stale value repeats the bug. A transaction that serializes the complete read-modify-write is another repair. Bound retries and distinguish a rejected condition from an ambiguous timeout after a successful commit.

## Check your understanding

- Distinguish operation linearizability from multi-operation atomicity.
- Offer atomic increment and versioned conditional write/transaction.
- Reread and recompute after a version conflict.

## Think one step further

What extra identity is needed if a client retries an atomic increment after an ambiguous timeout?

## Primary reading

- [Raft · extended paper](https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf)
objectives: Distinguish operation linearizability from multi-operation atomicity.
Offer atomic increment and versioned conditional write/transaction.

lessons.title: Retries need an atomic effect boundary
lessons.summary: Define exactly what a deduplication record protects
objectives: Define exactly what a deduplication record protects.
Handle a crash between effect and response.
lessons.body:
## Core idea

At-least-once delivery permits duplicates. A receiver can suppress duplicate logical requests when a stable identifier and effect are recorded atomically within a defined store. External effects outside that transaction need their own protocol. Deduplication history also has a retention boundary, and reusing an identifier for a different payload must be rejected or otherwise specified.

## Worked example

A job increments a database counter and records its request ID in one transaction. If the response is lost, a retry returns the stored result. Sending an email after that transaction still introduces a separate duplicate or missing-effect problem.

### Follow the steps

Start with counter 10 and an empty request log. Request r7 asks to increment by 1. In one transaction, store counter 11 and the result (r7, 11). Commit, then drop the response. A retry with r7 finds the saved result and returns 11 without incrementing again. A retry with r7 and a different amount should report a conflict if the contract binds IDs to payloads.

Now move the crash to before commit. The counter and request log should both remain unchanged. Draw a second timeline with a webhook sent between the write and commit. A rollback can undo the database writes while the webhook may already have arrived.

## Try it

Draw crash points for receive, validate, commit effect plus request ID, and respond. Add a second external sink and identify what the original transaction cannot guarantee.

## Check your work

The design does not claim global exactly-once execution. It defines payload identity, stored result behavior, retention, and the atomic boundary that makes duplicate suppression meaningful.

## Primary reading

Optional reading after the example and exercise.

- [PostgreSQL transaction tutorial](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/tutorial-transactions.html) · Review the all-or-nothing transaction boundary before tracing the separate webhook effect.

lessons.title: Leases express time; fencing enforces ownership
lessons.summary: Distinguish believing a lease is valid from enforcing current ownership
objectives: Distinguish believing a lease is valid from enforcing current ownership.
Place fencing checks at the protected resource.
lessons.body:
## Core idea

A lease grants time-bounded ownership under clock and timing assumptions. A paused client can resume after expiry and still attempt work. A monotonically ordered fencing token lets the protected resource reject older owners, provided it actually checks and remembers the appropriate token. A lock service alone cannot stop an external system from accepting stale writes.

## Worked example

Owner A receives token 10 and pauses. Owner B receives 11 and writes. When A resumes, a resource enforcing token order rejects 10. If A writes directly to an unfenced sink, the lock service’s newer lease does not prevent corruption.

### Follow the steps

Let a storage service remember the highest accepted token and the current value. A gets token 10, writes value a, and pauses. After its lease expires, B gets token 11 and writes value b. When A resumes, its write carries token 10. The storage service compares 10 with the stored 11 and rejects it without changing value b. Updating the stored token and value must share an atomic boundary.

Try restarting the storage service after B's write. If the service forgets token 11, it could accept A's stale write. Add a durable token check to your trace and repeat the test.

## Try it

Design a worker lease with token-based writes to a synthetic storage service. Include pauses, token persistence, and a resource that temporarily cannot reach the coordinator.

## Check your work

Enforcement occurs at each relevant effect boundary. State whether repeated operations with the same token are allowed and distinguish ownership ordering from operation deduplication.

## Primary reading

Optional reading after the example and exercise.

- [The Chubby lock service, §2.4](https://research.google.com/archive/chubby-osdi06.pdf) · Read the discussion of sequencers and how a resource can check a caller's lock generation.

lessons.title: Exactly once, within which boundary?
lessons.body:
## The problem to understand

Write pseudocode for an idempotent `POST /transfers` handler. The request contains a stable idempotency key and a source/destination/amount. Two identical retries may run concurrently. Balances and the idempotency table share one transactional database. Explain uniqueness, payload mismatch, result replay, insufficient funds, and the commit-before-response crash window.

```text
handleTransfer(key, source, destination, amount):
    // Give transaction-oriented pseudocode.
    // Include concurrent retry and crash behavior.
```

## The mental model

Use a unique constraint on the appropriately scoped idempotency key. Within a transaction, create/claim the key with a canonical request fingerprint, lock or conditionally update the affected balances, validate sufficient funds, and persist the terminal result. Commit the balances and result together. A concurrent loser waits/retries according to database behavior and reads the committed result; it must not apply the effect again.

The same key with a different fingerprint is a conflict. If the process crashes after commit but before responding, the retry returns the stored result. Decide whether validation/business failures are replayable terminal outcomes and retain keys for the advertised retry horizon. Do not perform an uncoordinated external side effect inside the handler and assume the database transaction makes it exactly once.

## Check your understanding

- Use a scoped unique key and canonical payload fingerprint.
- Commit balance effects and terminal result atomically.
- Handle concurrent retries, mismatch, and insufficient funds.
- Replay after commit-before-response and define retention boundaries.

## Think one step further

How would the design change if the destination balance lived in another database?

## Primary reading

- [Raft · extended paper](https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf)
objectives: Use a scoped unique key and canonical payload fingerprint.
Commit balance effects and terminal result atomically.

lessons.title: The old leader still answers
lessons.body:
## The problem to understand

A Raft leader becomes partitioned from a majority but can still serve a client. It has an old committed value and has not yet learned about a newer leader. Why is “read locally because I was elected leader” insufficient for linearizable reads? Describe a quorum-confirmed read approach and the additional assumptions required by a lease-based alternative.

## The mental model

An isolated former leader can continue believing it is leader while a majority elects another leader and commits newer writes. A local read may then return a value older than a completed write, violating linearizability. Past election authority is not proof of current authority.

A safe read-index style protocol establishes the leader’s current-term authority with a quorum and waits until the relevant committed index has been applied before serving the read. The leader also needs the protocol’s current-term commitment conditions; merely pinging any nodes is not a proof. Lease reads replace some communication with timing assumptions, requiring carefully bounded clock drift/lease behavior and correct interaction with elections and pauses. An unbounded process pause or unsound lease can restore the stale-leader problem.

## Check your understanding

- Construct the isolated old-leader/new-majority history.
- Confirm current authority with a quorum and wait for applied state.
- Recognize current-term protocol requirements.
- State timing/election assumptions behind lease alternatives.

## Think one step further

Why is a heartbeat sent only before a long read computation not necessarily enough to validate an arbitrary later response?

## Primary reading

- [Raft · extended paper](https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf)
objectives: Construct the isolated old-leader/new-majority history.
Confirm current authority with a quorum and wait for applied state.

lessons.title: Convergence requires a defined merge or repair rule
lessons.summary: Separate state repair from conflict resolution
objectives: Separate state repair from conflict resolution.
Choose conflict semantics that match the data type.
lessons.body:
## Core idea

Replicas can exchange missing state, but they still need semantics for concurrent updates. Last-writer-wins selects one value under a chosen timestamp order; it does not preserve every intent. CRDT designs use specific state and merge properties to converge under their assumptions. Deletions require metadata and retention rules so old replicas do not resurrect removed state.

## Worked example

Merging two independent plain integer counter values by maximum loses increments. A grow-only counter can instead track a component per writer and merge component-wise maxima, then sum, under a stable writer identity model.

## Try it

Simulate two replicas partitioning, incrementing a grow-only counter, and exchanging state in different orders with duplicates. Then explain why decrement or deletion needs a different design.

## Check your work

The merge is associative, commutative, and idempotent for the defined state. The explanation names metadata growth and identity assumptions instead of claiming every application can use the same merge rule.

## Primary reading

- [Raft extended paper](https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf)

lessons.title: Test histories under controlled faults
lessons.summary: Separate a test oracle from the implementation under test
objectives: Separate a test oracle from the implementation under test.
Exercise partitions, pauses, duplicates, and recovery reproducibly.
lessons.body:
## Core idea

Distributed tests need a failure schedule, observable operations, and an oracle for the promised guarantee. Inject faults at defined boundaries and record invocation/response histories. A deterministic simulator can explore many schedules but remains limited by its model. Real-process tests reveal additional I/O and deployment behavior. Use both types of evidence according to the claim.

## Worked example

A test pauses an old leader after it receives a request, elects another leader, then resumes the old one. The oracle checks that responses still admit the promised history and that stale ownership cannot produce forbidden effects.

## Try it

Write five fault schedules for a replicated register, including response loss after commitment and restart with a lagging log. State the invariant each schedule challenges.

## Check your work

The oracle does not merely compare internal variables with themselves. Seeds, message order, and observed histories are saved so a failed run can be replayed.

## Primary reading

- [Raft extended paper](https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf)

lessons.title: The lock expired. The old owner did not.
lessons.body:
## The problem to understand

Worker A holds a leased lock and begins writing to shared storage. It pauses long enough for the lease to expire. Worker B obtains the lock and starts its work. A resumes and continues writing. Design protection against stale-owner writes. Explain why checking the lease locally before a write is insufficient, and where monotonically increasing fencing tokens must be enforced.

## The mental model

A lease expiry does not stop the old process. A local check can become stale between checking and acting, especially across pauses or network delays. Issue a monotonically increasing fencing token when ownership is granted. Every protected storage operation carries the token, and the resource atomically rejects tokens older than the highest accepted epoch for that ownership domain.

Enforcement must live at the side-effect boundary, not only in the lock service or client. Define token scope, persistence across restarts, wrap/monotonicity behavior, and ordering of multi-step operations. B’s higher token prevents later writes from A once the resource advances its fence. If the resource cannot validate tokens, the lease alone does not provide this guarantee; use a transactional/conditional resource API or change the architecture. Idempotency is still needed for repeated operations within one epoch.

## Check your understanding

- Explain why expired leases do not revoke a paused process’s ability to act.
- Issue monotonically ordered ownership tokens.
- Enforce tokens atomically at the protected resource.
- Discuss persistence, token scope, and within-epoch idempotency.

## Think one step further

How would fencing work when the protected action is sending an email through a provider with no conditional-write API?

## Primary reading

- [Raft · extended paper](https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf)
objectives: Explain why expired leases do not revoke a paused process’s ability to act.
Issue monotonically ordered ownership tokens.

lessons.title: Capstone: a replicated register with a failure diary
lessons.summary: Integrate consistency, replication, retries, and recovery
objectives: Integrate consistency, replication, retries, and recovery.
Defend guarantees using histories and explicit assumptions.
lessons.body:
## Core idea

Build an educational state-machine simulator for a three-node replicated register, or use a maintained consensus library in a local service. Avoid presenting an incomplete custom protocol as production consensus. Specify read/write semantics, durable boundaries, retries, failure assumptions, and leadership behavior. Log every operation and injected fault.

## Worked example

A write commits but its response is lost. The client retries while a leader change occurs. Later, a paused old leader resumes. Your model must preserve acknowledged state and explain the result of every uncertain request.

### Starter exercise

Start with an event queue and three replica records. Each record needs a term, log, commit index, and applied value. Drive your model with this fixture.

1. Elect A, submit set x=5, and deliver enough messages to commit and acknowledge it.
2. Isolate A. Elect B with C, then submit and commit set x=8 on their side.
3. Heal the partition and deliver delayed messages from A. Let the replicas catch up.

The client may see 5 before the second write, but a successful linearizable read beginning after the second acknowledgement must see 8 if no later write exists. Assert that replicas never commit different values at the same index. Log the term and event that first violates an assertion.

## Try it

Deliver a protocol note, simulator or service, five reproducible fault schedules, and operation histories checked against the stated guarantee. Include a recovery trace and a list of excluded failures.

## Check your work

Review safety, liveness assumptions, atomic effect boundaries, and reproducibility. A passing small test suite is evidence within its model; document what remains unproven or delegated to the library.

## Primary reading

Optional reading after the example and exercise.

- [Raft paper, §5.4](https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf#page=8) · Compare the safety property and commit rule with the guarantees your simulator implements.

prerequisites: Understand processes, networking, concurrency, and basic data structures.
Be comfortable tracing state transitions and simple set intersections.
outcomes: Specify safety and liveness under a stated network and failure model.
Distinguish consistency guarantees using concrete operation histories.
Explain quorum, consensus, retry, and fencing assumptions.
Design and test a replicated service with explicit uncertain outcomes.
